lines.s: # pre-receive: the server runs this before any ref moves.
# Standard input has one line per proposed ref update: <old id> <new id> <ref name>
while read old new ref; do
refs/heads/main)                      # target of the branch rules
echo "rule 'restrict deletions': $ref may not be deleted"; status=1; continue
[ "$old" = "$zero" ] && continue    # creation: nothing to compare with
echo "rule 'block force pushes': the update would remove commits from $ref"; status=1
echo "rule 'require linear history': the update adds a merge commit to $ref"; status=1
refs/tags/v*)                         # target of the tag rules
echo "rule 'restrict deletions': $ref may not be deleted"; status=1
echo "rule 'restrict updates': $ref already exists and may not move"; status=1

beats.text: Two videos ago, the answer to "how did a force push get through" was a ruleset that had been left disabled. A force push, remember, replaces a branch on the server and can remove commits from it. Here is the other classic answer, and it is the one that fits most older repositories.
beats.tele: Two videos ago, the answer to "how did a force push get through" was a ruleset that had been left disabled. A force push, remember, replaces a branch on the server and can remove commits from it. Here is the other classic answer, and it is the one that fits most older repositories.

beats.text: main was protected by a classic branch protection rule, created years ago. The person who force-pushed was a repository administrator. And under a classic rule, administrators are not bound by default.
beats.tele: `main` was protected by a classic branch protection rule, created years ago. The person who force-pushed was a repository administrator. And under a classic rule, administrators are not bound by default.

beats.text: The rule was active. It targeted the right branch. It contained the right restriction. It did not apply to the person who pushed, and nobody on the team knew that, because only administrators can even see a classic rule.
